summary: Describes login referrals for IMAP4. When users are moved between servers, a server can redirect a client to the new home server so connecting still works. This helps sites with many users and many IMAP servers.

plainLanguage.summary: If you move to a new house, the old post office tells people your new address so they find you anyway. Your mail program is sent to the right server on its own.

questions: what is an imap login referral
how do imap clients get redirected to another server
subtitle: How an IMAP4 server can send a client to the server that actually holds the user's mailbox.

tldr.problem: Sites with many users and many IMAP4 servers sometimes move users between servers, and clients still need to find the right one.
tldr.mechanism: A server that advertises LOGIN-REFERRALS answers a login, an authentication, or a new connection with a REFERRAL response code carrying an IMAP URL for the user's home server.
tldr.outcome: The client connects directly to the new server, which is often more efficient than having the old server proxy the data and does not require it to impersonate the client.

today: RFC 2221 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Referrals
sections.content:
With many users and many IMAP4 servers, users sometimes have to move between servers, for example after hardware failures or organizational changes. Login referrals let clients transparently connect to the alternate server.

The alternative is the proxy method, in which the local server contacts the remote one for the client and relays the data. A referral gives the client a direct connection, which is often a better use of bandwidth and does not make the local server impersonate the client when it authenticates.

A home server holds the user's inbox; a remote server holds remote mailboxes.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one post office fetching your mail from another and handing it to you, you are simply told where to go yourself.

sections.title: How a Referral Is Given
sections.content:
A server supporting the extension MUST list LOGIN-REFERRALS in its CAPABILITY response; the client needs to do nothing to turn it on. The response code is REFERRAL and its argument MUST be a valid IMAP URL. A referral is a tagged NO or OK, or an untagged BYE.

A referral may answer a LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE command, or appear in the startup banner as BYE when the server will not accept connections. A tagged NO means the server has no mailboxes the user can access. A tagged OK means the personal mailboxes are elsewhere but public mailboxes here are readable. The client cannot tell whether the move is permanent or temporary.

A server SHOULD NOT refer to a server that will itself return a referral, and a client MUST NOT follow more than 10 levels of referral without consulting the user. URLs use user;AUTH=* so the client does not fall back to anonymous login.
sections.plainLanguage: When you knock at the wrong door, the answer is a note saying which door to try. You will not follow more than ten notes in a row without asking a grown-up.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The extension adds one alternative to the resp_text_code element of the IMAP4 grammar in RFC 2060: the word REFERRAL, a space, and an imapurl as defined in RFC 2192.
sections.plainLanguage: The only new thing in the message is the word REFERRAL followed by an address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Referrals use IMAP URLs, so they inherit the security considerations of URLs generally and of IMAP URLs in particular. A server MUST NOT give a referral if authentication for that user fails, to avoid revealing account information to an unauthorized person.

The mechanism could make it easier to write a rogue "password catching" server that collects login data and then refers the client to the real server. The RFC notes that the referral response also makes such an intrusion easier to detect.
sections.plainLanguage: A server only gives out the new address after you prove who you are. A fake server could trick you with a note too, but the note would be a clue that something is wrong.

messages.note: The client follows the URL directly.
